hints: Think about why ethane is so unreactive and what type of very reactive particle is needed to start a reaction with an alkane.
walkthrough:
Remember how alkanes behave**
Ethane is an alkane with only strong $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ sigma bonds and no pi electrons to attract electrophiles or nucleophiles. It does not react with polar reagents like acids or bases under normal conditions.

Spot the radical starter**
The only species in the list that can attack an alkane is the chlorine radical, $\text{Cl}$. It is highly reactive with an unpaired electron and can abstract a hydrogen atom from ethane to start free radical substitution to form chloroethane.

hints: Recall that the $\text{C=C}$ double bond is an electron rich region, so think about what type of reagent, electrophile or nucleophile, it will attract.
walkthrough:
See ethene as an electron donor**
The pi bond in ethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$, is a region of high electron density exposed above and below the molecule. It repels nucleophiles but strongly attracts electrophiles that can accept a pair of electrons.

Pick the electrophiles from the list**
Both $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ can supply $\text{H}^+$ to attack the pi bond in electrophilic addition. $\text{CN}^-$ and $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ are nucleophiles or bases, and $\text{Cl}$ radical attacks alkanes, so they do not fit here.
Final answer: $\text{HCl}$ AND $\text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Compare the acidity of propanoic acid and propan-1-ol and think about which species in the list acts as a base that only a stronger acid can protonate.
Recall the distinctive visible observation when a carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate to release a gas.
walkthrough:
Use the acidity difference**
Propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, is a weak acid but much stronger than the alcohol propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, which is effectively neutral. Carbonate ion, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, is a base strong enough to be protonated by the carboxylic acid but not by the alcohol.

Link to the observation**
With propanoic acid, $2\text{RCOOH} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{RCOO}^- + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, you see brisk effervescence as $\text{CO}_2$ gas bubbles off. With propan-1-ol there is no reaction, so no fizzing is seen, giving a clear distinction.

Final answer: $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$
Propanoic acid gives effervescence (of $\text{CO}_2$). Propan-1-ol gives no reaction / no observable change.

hints: Think about what energy source is needed to break the strong $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond to make two separate atoms.
walkthrough:
Supply energy to break Cl-Cl**
To convert $\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})$ into two $\text{Cl}(\text{g})$ atoms you must break a covalent bond, which needs energy. Ultraviolet light provides photons of exactly the right energy to be absorbed by $\text{Cl}_2$ and split the molecule.
Final answer: ultraviolet light / uv

hints: Focus on how the shared pair of electrons in $\text{Cl}_2$ splits when two identical radicals are formed, one electron going to each atom.
walkthrough:
Split the pair evenly**
In $\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}$, the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bonding pair divides so one electron goes to each chlorine atom. Because each product keeps one unpaired electron, this even splitting is called homolytic fission, the initiation step that makes radicals.
Final answer: homolytic fission (of chlorine / $\text{Cl}_2$)

hints: Think of the polar $\text{C=O}$ group where carbon is electron deficient and can be attacked by a nucleophile without leaving.
walkthrough:
Find the group that adds without losing**
Aldehydes and ketones contain the $\text{C=O}$ carbonyl group. Oxygen is more electronegative, so carbon carries a partial positive charge ($\delta+$). A nucleophile like $\text{CN}^-$ can add to this carbon, pushing pi electrons onto oxygen, with no atom leaving. This is nucleophilic addition.
Final answer: carbonyl / aldehyde / ketone

hints: Recall which type of halogenoalkane forms the most stable carbocation intermediate and so prefers the two step ionisation pathway.
walkthrough:
Connect SN1 to carbocation stability**
The $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ mechanism goes through a carbocation intermediate formed when the $\text{C-X}$ bond breaks first. Tertiary halogenoalkanes form tertiary carbocations, which are stabilised by electron donation from three alkyl groups, so they react readily by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ with nucleophiles.
Final answer: tertiary halogenoalkane

hints: Picture but-1-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$, and think about the two different carbons of the double bond that $\text{H}^+$ from the acid can add to.
Draw the carbocation left on the other carbon in each case, remembering to show the positive charge on carbon with only six electrons.
walkthrough:
Add H+ to make two routes**
But-1-ene is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. In acid hydration, $\text{H}^+$ adds to the $\text{C=C}$ to give a carbocation. If $\text{H}^+$ adds to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$ carbon, the positive charge ends up on carbon 2 to give the secondary ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{HCH}_3$.

Draw the alternative ion**
If $\text{H}^+$ adds instead to the internal $\text{CH}$ carbon, the positive charge ends up on carbon 1 to give the primary ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{H}_2$. These two different carbocations then react with water to give butan-2-ol and butan-1-ol, both $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{HCH}_3$ AND $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{H}_2$

hints: Identify which of the two ions from (d)(i) is secondary and which is primary by counting alkyl groups attached to the $\text{C}^+$.
Think about how alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon to spread and reduce the charge.
walkthrough:
Circle the secondary ion**
The more stable ion is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{HCH}_3$, the secondary carbocation. The other ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{H}_2$ is primary with only one alkyl group on $\text{C}^+$.

Explain with electron donation**
Alkyl groups are electron donating by the positive inductive effect. The secondary $\text{C}^+$ is joined to two alkyl groups ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ and $\text{CH}_3$) compared with only one for the primary ion. More electron density is pushed toward the electron deficient carbon, spreading the positive charge and lowering energy, so the secondary ion is more stable.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+\text{HCH}_3$ is more stable
It has more / 2 alkyl groups attached so it has the greater inductive / electron donating effect.
